implementation_notes: Without an HTTP framework the checkpoint is a guard object called by the request dispatcher before it routes to a handler; verification is delegated through an abstract Authenticator interface (virtual std::optional<Principal> verify(std::string_view credential)), injected so the mechanism can be swapped in tests and at configuration time. The guard owns the policy map and the challenge (401 response); the authenticator owns hashing, token parsing and constant-time comparison. Keep the guard framework-neutral only while no framework owns the HTTP stack - once one does, use its filter mechanism instead.
pitfalls: The guard must not own the credential store: an Authenticator that parses headers, hashes passwords and stores users recreates the coupling the pattern removes.
The principal must be request-scoped data (passed by reference into the request object); a shared member of the guard leaks identity between concurrent connections.

variants.name: Hand-written dispatch chokepoint

Keep the guard framework-neutral only while no framework owns the HTTP stack - once one does, use its filter mechanism instead.

variants.name: Crow middleware over crow::App
variants.implementation_notes: When the service runs on Crow, the checkpoint is a middleware class: a request-local context struct plus a before_handle(crow::request&, crow::response&, context&) hook that runs before the route handler, rejects with res.code = 401 followed by res.end(), or stores the verified principal in the context the handler receives. Middleware is listed on the application type (crow::App<AuthMiddleware>), so the protected surface is fixed per application, and the verifier is injected into the middleware as a service. This replaces the hand-written dispatcher guard once Crow owns the HTTP stack; prefer it over a custom chokepoint whenever the framework is already in use.
pitfalls: crow::response::end() is what stops the chain: forgetting it lets the request continue to the handler unauthenticated (fail-open).

Local (route-level) middleware and additional app instances can leave routes outside the guard; keep the authentication middleware at application level and treat route-level middleware as a deliberate exception.
